p.src: Now the man who had offered this plan was Mi Zhu, styled Zizhong, a native of Qu County in Donghai. His family had been wealthy for generations. Once, while returning by carriage from a trading journey to Luoyang, he met a beautiful woman who asked for a ride. Mi Zhu stepped down and continued on foot, yielding the carriage to her. The woman invited Mi Zhu to ride with her. Mi Zhu boarded and sat upright, never casting an improper glance at her. After they had traveled several li, the woman took her leave. As they parted, she said to Mi Zhu, “I am the Star Lord of the Fire Virtue of the South. By decree of the Supreme Lord, I am to burn down your home. Because you have treated me with courtesy, I tell you this plainly. Hurry home and remove your possessions. I shall come tonight.” When she had finished speaking, she vanished. Greatly alarmed, Mi Zhu raced home and hastily carried out everything in the house. That evening, sure enough, a fire broke out in the kitchen and burned the entire house to the ground. Thereafter Mi Zhu gave away his wealth freely, aiding the poor and relieving those in distress. Later, Tao Qian appointed him as an Assistant Officer. That day he proposed, “I am willing to go personally to Beihai Commandery and ask Kong Rong to raise troops to our aid. Let another man go to Tian Kai in Qingzhou to seek help. If troops from both places arrive together, Cao Cao will surely withdraw.” Tao Qian accepted the plan. He wrote two letters and asked which of his attendants dared go to Qingzhou to seek aid. One man immediately volunteered. All looked and saw Chen Deng, styled Yuanlong, a native of Guangling. Tao Qian first sent Chen Yuanlong off to Qingzhou, then ordered Mi Zhu to carry the letter to Beihai. He himself led his men in defending the city against attack.

p.src: Now Kong Rong of Beihai, styled Wenju, was a native of Qufu in the state of Lu. He was a twentieth-generation descendant of Confucius and the son of Kong Zhou, Commandant of Mount Tai. He had been intelligent from childhood. At the age of ten, he went to call upon Li Ying, Intendant of Henan. When the gatekeeper tried to turn him away, Kong Rong said, “My family and Lord Li’s are old family friends.” When he was admitted, Li Ying asked, “What kinship was there between your ancestor and mine?” Kong Rong replied, “Long ago Confucius asked Laozi about the rites. Does that not make your family and mine friends through many generations?” Li Ying marveled greatly at him. A little later, Chen Wei, Grand Master of the Palace, arrived. Pointing to Kong Rong, Li Ying said, “This is an extraordinary child.” Chen Wei said, “One who is clever in childhood may not necessarily be clever when grown.” Kong Rong instantly retorted, “Judging by what you say, sir, you must have been clever in childhood.” Chen Wei and the others all laughed and said, “When this child grows up, he will surely become a great man of his age.” From that time onward, he was renowned. Later he became General of the Household and, after successive promotions, Governor of Beihai. He delighted in entertaining guests and often said, “May the seats always be filled with guests and the wine jars never be empty—that is my wish.” During his six years in Beihai, he won the hearts of the people.

p.src: That day, while he was seated with guests, word came that Mi Zhu of Xuzhou had arrived. Kong Rong summoned him, asked why he had come, and Mi Zhu produced Tao Qian’s letter, saying, “Cao Cao presses the siege most fiercely. We beg Your Lordship to come to our aid.” Kong Rong said, “Tao Gongzu and I are close friends, and you, Zizhong, have come here in person. How could I refuse to go? But Cao Mengde bears me no enmity, so I should first send someone with a letter to mediate peace. If he will not agree, then I shall raise troops.” Mi Zhu said, “Cao Cao relies upon the might of his army and will certainly refuse peace.” Kong Rong ordered his troops mustered while a messenger was dispatched with the letter. While they were still discussing matters, a sudden report came that Guan Hai, a Yellow Turban remnant, was leading tens of thousands of bandits in a charge toward them. Kong Rong was greatly alarmed. He hastily mustered his own forces and marched out of the city to meet the bandits. Guan Hai rode forward and cried, “I know Beihai has abundant grain. Lend us ten thousand shi, and we shall withdraw at once. Otherwise, when we break into the city, neither old nor young shall be spared!” Kong Rong rebuked him: “I am a minister of the Great Han, guarding the Great Han’s land. How could I give grain to bandits?” Enraged, Guan Hai spurred his horse, brandished his saber, and charged straight at Kong Rong. Kong Rong’s officer Zong Bao rode out with his spear leveled. They had exchanged only a few bouts when Guan Hai struck Zong Bao from his horse with a single slash. Kong Rong’s troops fell into disorder and fled back into the city. Guan Hai divided his troops and surrounded the city on all sides, leaving Kong Rong deeply distressed. Mi Zhu’s grief and anxiety need hardly be told.

p.src: The next day, Kong Rong climbed the city wall and gazed into the distance. Seeing the immense strength of the bandits, his anxiety doubled. Suddenly he saw a lone rider outside the city, spear leveled, charging into the bandit ranks. He dashed left and right as though through deserted ground, fought his way directly beneath the wall, and shouted, “Open the gate!” Kong Rong did not recognize the man and dared not open the gate. When the bandits pursued him to the riverside, the man wheeled around and thrust more than ten of them from their horses. The bandits recoiled, and Kong Rong hurriedly ordered the gate opened and the man admitted. The man dismounted and laid aside his spear, went straight up onto the wall, and paid his respects to Kong Rong. Asked his name, he replied, “I am a native of Huang County in Donglai. My compound surname is Taishi, my given name Ci, and my style Ziyi. My aged mother has repeatedly received your gracious care. Yesterday I returned from Liaodong to visit her. When I learned the bandits had besieged the city, my mother said, ‘We have repeatedly received the Governor’s great kindness. You must go to his aid.’ Therefore I came alone on horseback.” Kong Rong was overjoyed. In fact, though Kong Rong and Taishi Ci had never met, Kong Rong knew him by reputation as a hero. Because Taishi Ci had been away and his aged mother lived twenty li outside the city, Kong Rong had often sent her grain and silk. Grateful for Kong Rong’s virtue, his mother had expressly sent her son to the rescue.

p.src: Kong Rong treated Taishi Ci with great honor and presented him with clothing, armor, a saddle, and a horse. Taishi Ci said, “Lend me a thousand picked troops, and I shall go out and destroy the bandits.” Kong Rong replied, “Though you are brave, the bandits are overwhelmingly strong. You must not venture out rashly.” Taishi Ci said, “My mother, grateful for your great virtue, sent me here expressly. If I cannot lift the siege, I shall have no face to see her again. I beg leave to fight to the death.” Kong Rong said, “I have heard that Liu Xuande is a hero of this age. If he could be asked to come to our aid, this siege would be lifted. But there is no one I can send.” Taishi Ci replied, “Write the letter, Governor, and I shall hasten there.” Delighted, Kong Rong wrote a letter and entrusted it to Taishi Ci. Taishi Ci donned his armor and mounted, with bow and arrows at his waist and iron spear in hand. After eating his fill and making every preparation, he flew alone through the opened gate. Near the river, bandit officers led their men against him. Taishi Ci thrust several of them dead and broke through the encirclement. Learning that someone had left the city, Guan Hai guessed he must be going for reinforcements. He personally led several hundred horsemen in pursuit and surrounded Taishi Ci on every side. Taishi Ci rested his spear, took up his bow, set an arrow to the string, and shot in every direction. Every shaft brought a rider down. The bandits dared pursue no farther. Having escaped, Taishi Ci rode through the night to Pingyuan to meet Liu Xuande. After exchanging courtesies, he gave a full account of how Kong Rong of Beihai was besieged and sought aid, then presented the letter. When Xuande had finished reading it, he asked Taishi Ci, “Who are you, sir?” Taishi Ci replied, “I am Taishi Ci, an obscure man of Donghai. Kong Rong and I are neither blood kin nor fellow townsmen; we are bound only by shared principles and friendship, and by a desire to share each other’s troubles and dangers. Now Guan Hai has risen in violence, Beihai is besieged, and Kong Rong stands alone with nowhere to appeal, in peril from one dawn to the next. Knowing your benevolence and righteousness have long been renowned, and that you rescue those in peril, he sent me expressly to brave the blades, break through the encirclement, and come seek your aid.” Xuande’s expression grew solemn as he replied, “Does Kong Rong of Beihai know that Liu Bei exists in this world?” He then mustered three thousand picked troops with Yunchang and Yide and set out for Beihai Commandery.

p.src: When Guan Hai saw the relief force arrive, he personally led his troops out to meet it; seeing that Xuande had few men, he thought nothing of them. Xuande, Guan Yu, Zhang Fei, and Taishi Ci reined in their horses before the battle line, and Guan Hai charged straight out in fury. Taishi Ci was about to advance, but Guan Yu had already ridden forth and made straight for Guan Hai. As the two horses met, the armies raised a tremendous shout; but how could Guan Hai withstand Guan Yu? Within a few dozen bouts, the Green Dragon blade flashed and cleft Guan Hai from his horse. Taishi Ci and Zhang Fei spurred out together; raising their two spears, they plunged into the rebels' ranks. Xuande drove his troops forward in a sweeping attack. From the city walls, Kong Rong saw Taishi Ci, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei pursuing and slaughtering the rebels like tigers among a flock of sheep, ranging wherever they pleased with none able to withstand them, and at once led his troops out of the city. Attacked from both sides, the rebels suffered a crushing defeat; countless men surrendered, and the rest scattered in rout.

p.src: Kong Rong welcomed Xuande into the city and, after the customary courtesies, laid out a great banquet in celebration. He also brought Mi Zhu forward to meet Xuande and had him relate in full how Zhang Kai had murdered Cao Song: “Cao Cao is now letting his troops plunder without restraint and has surrounded Xuzhou. I have come expressly to seek aid.” Xuande said, “Tao Gongzu is a humane and honorable gentleman. I never imagined he would suffer such an undeserved calamity.” Kong Rong said, “You are a kinsman of the imperial house. Now Cao Cao is slaughtering the common people and using his strength to oppress the weak. Why not come with me to their rescue?” Xuande said, “I would not dare refuse, but my soldiers are few and my officers scarce, so I fear I cannot move lightly.” Kong Rong said, “My desire to save Tao Gongzu arises partly from our old friendship, but also from the greater cause of righteousness. Can it be that you alone have no heart to uphold what is right?” Xuande said, “If that is so, please go on ahead, Wenju. Allow me to visit Gongsun Zan and borrow three or five thousand troops; I shall follow at once.” Kong Rong said, “You must not break your word.” Xuande said, “What sort of man do you take me for? The Sage said, ‘Death has been with us from of old, but without trust no man can stand.’ Whether Liu Bei succeeds in borrowing troops or not, he will assuredly come in person.” Kong Rong assented; he told Mi Zhu to return first to Xuzhou with the news, then made his own preparations to depart. Taishi Ci bowed in gratitude and said, “I came at my mother's command to lend you aid, and happily you are now out of danger. The Inspector of Yangzhou, Liu Yao, who comes from my own commandery, has sent a letter summoning me, and I dare not fail to go. May we meet again another day.” Kong Rong offered him gold and silk in recompense, but Taishi Ci refused them and returned home. When his mother saw him, she said joyfully, “I am glad that you have found a way to repay Beihai!” She then sent Taishi Ci on his way to Yangzhou.

p.src: Meanwhile, Mi Zhu returned and reported to Tao Qian that Beihai had also secured Liu Xuande's aid; Chen Yuanlong likewise returned with word that Tian Kai of Qingzhou had gladly agreed to lead troops to the rescue; and Tao Qian's mind was eased. As it happened, the two forces under Kong Rong and Tian Kai feared the might of Cao Cao's army; they encamped far off beneath the hills and dared not advance rashly. When Cao Cao saw the two armies arrive, he too divided his forces and did not dare press forward to attack the city.

p.src: When Liu Xuande's army arrived, he went to see Kong Rong. Kong Rong said, “Cao Cao's forces are formidable, and Cao Cao himself is skilled in the use of troops. We must not engage him lightly. Let us first observe his movements, and then advance.” Xuande said, “I fear only that there is no grain within the city and that it cannot hold out for long. I shall order Guan Yu and Zilong to lead four thousand troops and serve under your command; I myself will take Zhang Fei, charge through Cao Cao's camp, and make straight for Xuzhou to consult with Governor Tao.” Kong Rong was delighted. He joined forces with Tian Kai so that their camps supported each other like two horns; Guan Yu and Zilong led troops in support on either flank. That day, Xuande and Zhang Fei led a thousand horse and foot in an assault upon the edge of Cao Cao's encampment. As they advanced, a drum suddenly thundered within the camp, and cavalry and infantry surged out like tides and waves. At their head was the great commander Yu Jin, who reined in his horse and shouted, “Who are you mad rogues? Where do you think you are going?” At the sight of him, Zhang Fei wasted no words but charged straight at Yu Jin. Their horses met, and after several bouts Xuande drew his paired swords and waved his troops into a great advance; Yu Jin turned and fled. Zhang Fei pursued and slew at the fore, driving the enemy all the way to the walls of Xuzhou. From the walls they saw a red banner bearing white characters that read in large script, “Liu Xuande of Pingyuan,” and Tao Qian hastily ordered the gates opened. Xuande entered the city, where Tao Qian received him, and together they went to the government offices. After the courtesies were completed, a banquet was laid for him while the troops were rewarded and refreshed.

Xuande said in astonishment, “What do you mean by this?” Tao Qian said, “The realm is now in turmoil and royal authority has fallen into decay. I shall personally draft a memorial and submit it to the court.” Xuande left his seat, bowed twice, and said, “Though Liu Bei is a descendant of the Han, his merit is slight and his virtue meager. Even as Chancellor of Pingyuan, I fear I am unequal to my office. I have come now to lend aid solely for the sake of righteousness. By speaking thus, can it be that you suspect Liu Bei of harboring designs to annex your territory? If I have entertained such a thought, may Heaven deny me its protection!” Tao Qian said, “These are my true feelings.” He offered Xuzhou again and again, but Xuande would by no means accept it. Mi Zhu stepped forward and said, “The enemy is now at the city walls. For the present, we should discuss a plan to repel them. When the crisis has passed, you may raise the matter of yielding the province again.” Xuande said, “I shall send Cao Cao a letter and urge him to make peace and withdraw. If he refuses, it will not be too late to fight.” Accordingly, orders were sent to the three encampments to hold their troops and make no move for the time being; and a messenger was dispatched to deliver the letter to Cao Cao.

p.src: Meanwhile, as Cao Cao was conferring with his commanders in camp, a man reported that a letter of challenge had arrived from Xuzhou. Cao Cao opened and read it; it was a letter from Liu Bei. It read in essence: “Since I was privileged to behold your honored countenance beyond the passes, Heaven has placed us in separate quarters, and I have had no opportunity to attend upon you. Recently your honored father, Lord Cao, met his death solely through Zhang Kai's wickedness; Tao Gongzu was not to blame. At present the remnants of the Yellow Scarves are causing disorder without; while the remnants of Dong Zhuo's faction remain entrenched within. I pray that you, illustrious lord, will place the court's urgent peril before your private vengeance; withdraw your forces from Xuzhou and relieve the nation's distress. Then great indeed will be the good fortune of Xuzhou and of all the realm!” After reading the letter, Cao Cao cursed loudly: “Who is Liu Bei, that he dares send a letter to admonish me? And it contains barbs of mockery besides!” He ordered the messenger beheaded and commanded an all-out assault upon the city. Guo Jia remonstrated: “Liu Bei has come from afar to give aid, first observing courtesy before resorting to arms. My lord should answer him with gracious words, thereby lulling his vigilance; then advance and attack the city, and it can be taken.” Cao Cao followed his counsel, treated the messenger courteously, and kept him there while awaiting the dispatch of a reply.

p.src: While they were still deliberating, a courier on a fleet horse suddenly galloped in with news of disaster. Cao Cao asked what had happened and was told that Lü Bu had already taken Yanzhou by surprise and advanced to occupy Puyang. It transpired that after Lü Bu became embroiled in the turmoil caused by Li Jue and Guo Si, he fled through Wuguan and went to seek refuge with Yuan Shu; but Yuan Shu distrusted Lü Bu's constant treachery and refused to receive him. Lü Bu then went to Yuan Shao, who accepted him, and together they defeated Zhang Yan at Changshan; believing that he had attained his ambitions, Lü Bu treated Yuan Shao's officers and soldiers with arrogance. Yuan Shao sought to kill him, so Lü Bu left and sought refuge with Zhang Yang, who received him.

p.src: At this time, Pang Shu was in Chang’an, where he secretly sheltered Lü Bu’s wife and children and sent them back to him. When Li Jue and Guo Si learned of it, they had Pang Shu beheaded, then wrote to Zhang Yang ordering him to kill Lü Bu. Lü Bu therefore left Zhang Yang and went to seek refuge with Zhang Miao. Just then, Zhang Miao’s younger brother Zhang Chao brought Chen Gong to meet Zhang Miao. Chen Gong said to Zhang Miao, “The realm is now breaking apart and heroes are rising everywhere. Though you command the forces of a thousand-li domain, you submit to another man’s control. Is that not contemptible? Cao Cao has now marched east, leaving Yan Province undefended, while Lü Bu is the foremost warrior of our age. If you join him in taking Yan Province, you may lay the foundations of hegemony.” Zhang Miao was overjoyed. He promptly ordered Lü Bu to launch a surprise attack and seize Yan Province, after which Lü Bu occupied Puyang. Only the three places of Juancheng, Dong’e, and Fan County remained intact, preserved by the schemes and desperate defense of Xun Yu and Cheng Yu; all the rest fell. Cao Ren fought repeatedly but could win no victory, and so he sent this urgent appeal. Cao Cao was greatly alarmed by the report. “If Yan Province is lost, I shall have no home to return to. I must recover it at once!” Guo Jia said, “My lord, this is the perfect occasion to do Liu Bei a favor: withdraw your army and return to recover Yan Province.” Cao Cao approved. He immediately sent a reply to Liu Bei, struck camp, and withdrew his troops.

p.src: Meanwhile, the envoy returned to Xu Province, entered the city, and presented Tao Qian with the letter, reporting that Cao Cao’s army had withdrawn. Tao Qian was delighted and sent men to invite Kong Rong, Tian Kai, Guan Yu, Zhao Yun, and the others to a grand gathering in the city. When the banquet was over, Tao Qian invited Xuande to the seat of honor, clasped his hands, and addressed the assembly: “I am old, and my two sons lack ability; they are unequal to the grave responsibilities of governing the realm. Lord Liu is a scion of the imperial house, broad in virtue and eminent in talent, and is fit to govern Xu Province. I wish only to retire and tend to my illness.” Xuande replied, “Kong Wenju bade me come to the aid of Xu Province, and I did so for righteousness’ sake. If I now seize it without cause and make it my own, the whole realm will condemn me as a man without honor.” Mi Zhu said, “The Han house is now in decline, and all within the seas is in turmoil. This is precisely the time to accomplish great deeds and establish a lasting enterprise. Xu Province is rich and prosperous, with a million households. Lord Liu must govern it; you cannot refuse.” Xuande said, “I absolutely dare not accept.” Chen Deng said, “Governor Tao is often ill and cannot attend to official affairs. My lord, pray do not decline.” Xuande said, “Yuan Gonglu descends from a family that produced the Three Excellencies for four generations, and all within the seas look to him. He is nearby at Shouchun; why not yield the province to him?” Kong Rong said, “Yuan Gonglu is nothing but a withered bone in a grave—not worth mentioning! In the matter before you today, if you do not take what Heaven bestows, regret will come too late.”

p.src: Xuande remained adamant and would not consent. Tao Qian wept and said, “If you abandon me and depart, I shall die with my eyes unclosed!” Guan Yu said, “Since Lord Tao has offered it to you, elder brother, you might take temporary charge of the province’s affairs.” Zhang Fei said, “It is not as though we were trying to take his province and commanderies by force. He offers them of his own goodwill—why refuse so stubbornly?” Xuande said, “Would you have me fall into unrighteousness?” Tao Qian pressed the offer again and again, but Xuande would not accept. Tao Qian said, “If Xuande is truly unwilling to consent, there is a nearby town called Xiaopei, which would serve well as a garrison. Would you agree to station your army there for the present and protect Xu Province?” Everyone urged Xuande to remain at Xiaopei, and he agreed. After Tao Qian had rewarded the troops, Zhao Yun took his leave. Xuande clasped his hand, and they parted in tears. Kong Rong and Tian Kai likewise said their farewells and led their armies home. Xuande, together with Guan Yu and Zhang Fei, led his own troops to Xiaopei, repaired its walls, and reassured its inhabitants.

p.src: When Lü Bu learned that Cao Cao’s returning army had already passed Teng County, he summoned his deputy commanders Xue Lan and Li Feng and said, “I have long wished to put you two to use. Take ten thousand men and hold Yan Province firmly. I shall personally lead the troops forward to defeat Cao Cao.” The two men accepted the command. Chen Gong hurried in and asked, “General, if you abandon Yan Province, where do you intend to go?” Lü Bu replied, “I mean to station my army at Puyang and establish a three-cornered balance of power.” Chen Gong said, “That is a mistake. Xue Lan will certainly be unable to hold Yan Province. One hundred and eighty li due south of here, the road through Mount Tai is perilous. Ten thousand elite troops could be concealed there. When Cao Cao’s soldiers hear that Yan Province is lost, they will surely advance at double speed. Wait until half their force has passed, then strike once, and they can be captured.” Lü Bu said, “I have another excellent plan for stationing my forces at Puyang. What could you know of it?” Thus he rejected Chen Gong’s counsel, left Xue Lan to defend Yan Province, and departed.

p.src: Meanwhile, Cao Cao’s army drew near Puyang and established its camp. The next day, he led out his generals and arrayed the troops in the open country. Cao Cao reined in beneath his commander’s banner and watched Lü Bu’s army approach from afar. When Lü Bu’s formation had closed into a circle, he rode out in the lead. Eight valiant generals were arrayed on either side of him. The first was a native of Mayi in Yanmen, surnamed Zhang, named Liao, and styled Wenyuan. The second was a native of Huayin in Taishan, surnamed Zang, named Ba, and styled Xuangao. These two generals were accompanied by six more valiant commanders: Hao Meng, Cao Xing, Cheng Lian, Wei Xu, Song Xian, and Hou Cheng. Lü Bu’s army numbered fifty thousand, and the thunder of its drums shook the field. Pointing at Lü Bu, Cao Cao said, “There has never been any feud between us. Why did you seize my province and commanderies?” Lü Bu replied, “The cities of the Han belong to all men. Why should you alone possess them?” He then ordered Zang Ba to ride out and challenge the enemy. Yue Jin rode out from Cao Cao’s ranks to meet him. The two horses met, and both spears rose together. They fought for more than thirty bouts, with neither gaining the upper hand. Xiahou Dun spurred forward to join the fight, but Zhang Liao intercepted him from Lü Bu’s formation and engaged him in combat. Lü Bu’s temper flared. Leveling his halberd, he drove his horse out from the formation, and both Xiahou Dun and Yue Jin fled. Lü Bu pressed the pursuit, routing Cao Cao’s army and driving it back thirty or forty li. Lü Bu then recalled his troops.

p.src: After losing the battle, Cao Cao returned to camp and conferred with his generals. Yu Jin said, “Today I climbed a hill to survey the country. West of Puyang, Lü Bu has a camp that appears to contain few troops. Tonight they will suppose our army has fled in defeat and will surely be unprepared. We can lead troops against it. p.src: Now Cao Cao led his army to the western camp at dusk and stormed it from all sides. The camp's defenders could not withstand the assault and fled in every direction, leaving Cao Cao to seize the camp. Near the fourth watch, Gao Shun finally arrived with his troops and fought his way into the camp. Cao Cao personally led his forces out to meet him and encountered Gao Shun head-on; the armies plunged into a confused battle. As dawn approached, drums thundered due west, and a messenger reported that Lü Bu himself was coming at the head of an army. Cao Cao abandoned the camp and fled. Gao Shun, Wei Xu, and Hou Cheng pursued him from behind, while Lü Bu himself approached at the head of his troops from the front. Yu Jin and Yue Jin together engaged Lü Bu but could not hold him, so Cao Cao made northward. Another body of troops emerged from behind the hills, with Zhang Liao on the left and Zang Ba on the right. Cao Cao sent Lü Qian and Cao Hong against them, but they fared poorly, and he fled westward. Suddenly, great battle cries erupted once more as another force arrived: the four generals Hao Meng, Cao Xing, Cheng Lian, and Song Xian blocked the road ahead. The generals fought desperately, while Cao Cao charged the enemy lines at their head. At the clatter of the wooden signal, arrows came flying like a sudden downpour.

p.src: Unable to advance and seeing no way of escape, Cao Cao cried out, “Who will save me?” A general leapt forth from among the cavalry: it was Dian Wei. Brandishing a pair of iron halberds, he shouted, “My lord, have no fear!” He sprang from his horse, planted his two halberds in the ground, took more than ten short javelins and tucked them in his hand, then told his attendants, “Call out to me only when the enemy comes within ten paces!” Then, breaking into a run, he advanced through the hail of arrows. Several dozen of Lü Bu's horsemen pursued him, and his attendants cried, “They are ten paces away!” Dian Wei said, “Call out only when they are five paces away!” The attendant called again, “They are five paces away!” Dian Wei then hurled his javelins at them. With each cast, a man fell from his horse; not one missed its mark, and in moments he had killed more than ten men. The rest all fled. Dian Wei sprang back onto his horse, raised his pair of great iron halberds, and charged into the enemy. The four generals Hao Meng, Cao Xing, Cheng Lian, and Song Xian could not withstand him and each fled for his life. Dian Wei scattered the enemy and rescued Cao Cao. u.src: Unable to advance and seeing no way of escape, Cao Cao cried out, “Who will save me?”
A general leapt forth from among the cavalry: it was Dian Wei.
Brandishing a pair of iron halberds, he shouted, “My lord, have no fear!”

He sprang from his horse, planted his two halberds in the ground, took more than ten short javelins and tucked them in his hand, then told his attendants, “Call out to me only when the enemy comes within ten paces!”
Then, breaking into a run, he advanced through the hail of arrows.
Several dozen of Lü Bu's horsemen pursued him, and his attendants cried, “They are ten paces away!”
Dian Wei said, “Call out only when they are five paces away!”
The attendant called again, “They are five paces away!”
Dian Wei then hurled his javelins at them. With each cast, a man fell from his horse; not one missed its mark, and in moments he had killed more than ten men.
The rest all fled.
